# The Candle as a Way into Natural Philosophy

The speaker opens his course with a plain statement of purpose. Over these lectures he intends to present the chemical history of a candle. He offers the lectures in return for the honour the audience does him by coming to see the proceedings, treating the exchange as a courtesy owed rather than a performance given.

## Why Return to the Candle

This is not new ground for him. He has lectured on this subject on a former occasion, and he admits that if he were left to his own will he would repeat it almost every year. His reason is that the subject of the candle holds abundant interest. It is not a narrow topic. The candle opens onto many different departments of philosophy, and the reach of the subject is wider still: every law governing any part of the universe comes into play in the phenomena of a candle.

From this he draws a methodological conclusion. Studying the physical phenomena of a candle is the best and most open way into the study of natural philosophy. A beginner needs no specialised apparatus to start, only attention to something burning in front of him. The speaker therefore does not apologise for an old topic. In his judgment no newer topic would be better than the candle, and probably none would be as good.

## Tone and Audience

He sets out the terms on which he will proceed. He intends to treat the subject honestly, seriously, and philosophically. He also declares his chosen audience: he means to address the young people rather than the adults in the room. He claims the privilege of speaking to young people as a young person himself, and he notes that he has addressed young audiences in this way on former occasions. He is aware that his words will be published to the world, but that knowledge will not stop him from speaking familiarly to the young listeners in front of him.

## Natural Candles: Candle-Wood

Before turning to manufactured candles, the speaker remarks that some candles are great curiosities, and that some kinds of trees are particularly famous for burning well. His chief example is a substance called candle-wood, taken from some bogs in Ireland.

Candle-wood is a hard, strong, excellent wood, well suited to resisting force, and it also burns well. Where it is found, people make splinters and torches from it. It burns like a candle and gives a very good light. For these reasons the speaker regards it as one of the best illustrations of the general nature of a candle.

Its value as an illustration comes from the functions it performs. Candle-wood provides fuel. It provides a means of bringing that fuel to the place of chemical action. It provides a regular and gradual supply of air to the same place. And it produces heat and light. Because it combines all of these functions in one material, candle-wood is in effect a natural candle, and it serves as a reference model for the manufactured candles that follow.

## Dips

The first manufactured type is the candle commonly called a dip. Dips are made by hanging lengths of cotton by a loop and dipping them in melted tallow. Each length is then cooled and re-dipped, over and over, until tallow builds up around the cotton.

## Miners' Candles

Very small candles were used by miners in coal mines. In former times miners had to supply their own candles. It was believed that a small candle would ignite fire-damp in the mines less readily than a large one, so miners used small candles partly for safety and partly for economy. These candles were made at 20, 30, 40, or 60 to the pound. In time they were replaced by the steel-mill, and the steel-mill was later replaced by the Davy lamp and other safety lamps.

## A Candle from the Royal George

The speaker's next specimen concerns durability. Colonel Pasley reportedly took a candle from the wreck of the Royal George. It had been sunk in the sea and exposed to salt water for many years. The example demonstrates that candles can be preserved well over long periods. Although this candle is cracked and broken, it burns regularly when lit, and its tallow returns to its natural condition once melted.

## Materials and the Stearin Process

The speaker credits Mr. Field of Lambeth with supplying him with many illustrations of candles and their materials. He then turns to those materials.

The first is suet, which is the fat of the ox. The speaker believes Russian tallow is used to make dips. A significant advance came when Gay-Lussac, or someone who shared the knowledge with him, converted tallow into stearin. The practical difference is visible in use. Modern candles are clean rather than greasy like ordinary tallow candles. The drips from a modern candle can be scraped off and powdered without soiling anything.

The conversion proceeds in stages:

1. **Saponification.** Tallow is first boiled with quicklime to make a soap.
2. **Acid decomposition.** The soap is then decomposed with sulphuric acid, which removes the lime. This decomposition leaves the fat rearranged as stearic acid.
3. **By-product.** Glycerin is produced at the same time as the stearic acid. Glycerin is a sugar, or a substance similar to sugar, and it comes out of the tallow during this chemical change.
4. **Pressing.** The oil is then pressed out of the stearic acid. As the pressure increases, the oily part carries the impurities out with it.
5. **Casting.** The substance left after pressing is melted and cast into candles.

The products of this process are stearin candles, made from stearin derived from tallow.

## Other Candle Materials

The speaker closes this survey with the remaining materials. Sperm candles come from the purified oil of the spermaceti whale. Candles are also made from yellow beeswax and from refined beeswax. Paraffin is a curious substance from which candles are made, and it can be obtained from the bogs of Ireland. Finally, a kind of wax brought from Japan is a new material for making candles; it became available only after Japan was forced open to outside access.

# The Candle as a Way into Natural Philosophy

In return for the honour you do me in coming to see what we are about, I propose to bring before you, in the course of these lectures, the Chemical History of a Candle. I count the lectures as a courtesy which I owe you for that honour, and I do not offer them as a performance.

I have taken up this subject on a former occasion. If it were left to my own will, I should repeat it almost every year, so abundant is the interest which attaches to it. The candle is a wide subject. It opens upon many different departments of philosophy; and there is not a law under which any part of this universe is governed which does not come into play in the phenomena of a candle.

Hence there is no better and no more open door by which we can enter into the study of natural philosophy than the consideration of the physical phenomena of a candle. The beginner wants no special apparatus. A candle burning before him, and his attention fixed upon it, are enough to set him on his way. I make no apology, therefore, for returning to an old topic. A newer one would not be better than the candle, and in all probability it would not be so good.

Before going further, I would set down the terms on which I mean to proceed. I intend to treat the matter honestly, seriously, and philosophically. I also claim the privilege of speaking to the young people in the room rather than to their elders, and I claim it as a young person myself, having addressed young hearers in this familiar way on former occasions. What is said here will be published to the world; yet the knowledge of that shall not deter me from speaking familiarly to the young listeners who sit before me now.

Some candles are great curiosities, and certain kinds of trees have become particularly famous for the readiness with which they burn. Of these the best instance I can give is a substance called candle-wood, which is got out of some of the bogs of Ireland.

Candle-wood is a hard, strong, excellent wood, well fitted to resist force, and it burns well besides. Where it is found, the people make splinters and torches of it, for it burns like a candle and gives a very good light. I know of few better illustrations of the general nature of a candle.

Its value as an illustration lies in what it does. In it we have the fuel; we have the means of bringing that fuel to the place of chemical action; we have a regular and gradual supply of air to the same place; and we have the heat and light which are produced there. Since a single material discharges all of these offices, candle-wood is in effect a natural candle, and we may take it as the model against which the manufactured candles are to be measured.

Of manufactured candles, the first is the one commonly called a dip. To make it, lengths of cotton are hung up by a loop and dipped into melted tallow. Each is then taken out and cooled, and dipped again, and the cooling and re-dipping go on, time after time, until tallow has built up round the cotton.

Very small candles were used by the miners in coal mines. In former times the miner had to find his own candles, and it was supposed that a small candle would not so readily set fire to the fire-damp in the mines as a large one; so the miners chose them small, partly for safety and partly for economy. They were made at 20, 30, 40, or 60 to the pound. In time the steel-mill displaced them, and the steel-mill was in its turn displaced by the Davy lamp and other safety lamps.

The next specimen bears upon durability. This candle, I am told, was taken by Colonel Pasley from the wreck of the Royal George. The ship went down in the sea, and the candle lay exposed to salt water for many years. It shows how well a candle may keep over long periods. Though it is cracked and broken, it burns regularly when lighted, and its tallow, once melted, returns to its natural condition.

For a great many illustrations of candles, and of the materials of which they are made, I am indebted to Mr. Field of Lambeth.

The first of those materials is suet, the fat of the ox, and Russian tallow, I believe, is employed in the making of dips. A considerable advance was made when Gay-Lussac, or some one who shared the knowledge with him, converted tallow into stearin. The difference is plain in use. A modern candle is clean, where an ordinary tallow candle is greasy, and the drippings from a modern candle may be scraped off and beaten into powder without soiling anything.

The conversion of tallow into stearin is carried out in several stages.

The tallow is first boiled with quicklime, and a soap is made of it. This soap is then decomposed by sulphuric acid, which takes away the lime and leaves the fat rearranged as stearic acid. Along with the stearic acid there is produced a quantity of glycerin, which is a sugar, or a substance like sugar, and which comes out of the tallow in the course of this chemical change. The oil is next pressed out of the stearic acid; and as the pressure is increased, the oily part carries the impurities away with it. What remains after pressing is melted and cast into candles.

The candles so obtained are the stearin candles, made of stearin which has been derived from tallow.

There remain the other materials. Sperm candles come from the purified oil of the spermaceti whale. Candles are made, too, from yellow beeswax and from refined beeswax. Paraffin, a curious substance which may be obtained from the bogs of Ireland, also yields candles. Lastly, there is a kind of wax brought from Japan, a new material for the candle-maker, which has reached us only since Japan was forced open to the outside world.

candidates.text:
# The Candle as a Way into Natural Philosophy

It is my purpose, in return for the honour which you do me by coming to see our proceedings here, to bring before you, in the course of these lectures, the chemical history of a candle. I regard the lectures as a courtesy which I owe to you for that honour, and I offer them in that spirit; they are a debt to be discharged, and I do not intend them as a performance.

## Why Return to the Candle

I have taken this subject on a former occasion; and were it left to my own will, I should repeat it almost every year, so abundant is the interest which attaches to it. The candle is by no means a narrow topic. It opens, in the most remarkable manner, upon many different departments of philosophy; and its reach is wider still, for there is not a law under which any part of this universe is governed which does not come into play in the phenomena of a candle.

Hence there is no better and no more open door by which we may enter into the study of natural philosophy than the physical phenomena of a candle. The beginner who would pass through that door needs no special apparatus to carry with him; it is enough that he should attend to the thing which burns before him. I make no apology, therefore, for returning to an old subject. Were we to search among newer topics for a starting point, we should find none better than the candle, and probably none so good.

## Tone and Audience

Let me state the terms upon which I mean to proceed. We shall treat the subject honestly, seriously, and philosophically. I purpose, moreover, to address myself to the young people present rather than to their elders; and I claim the privilege of speaking to the young as a young person myself, as I have done on former occasions when they formed my audience. I am aware that what is said here will be published to the world; but that knowledge shall not deter me from speaking familiarly to the young listeners who sit nearest to me in this room.

## Natural Candles: Candle-Wood

Before we come to the candles of the manufacturer, it may be remarked that some candles are great curiosities, and that certain kinds of trees are particularly famous for burning well. The chief instance I can offer is a substance called _candle-wood_, which is taken out of some of the bogs in Ireland, and which is an excellent example of a wood that burns well.

Candle-wood is a hard, strong, excellent wood, well fitted to resist force; and with this strength it combines the property of burning well. Where it is found, the people split it into splinters and make torches of it, and these burn like a candle and give a very good light. For such reasons we may take candle-wood as one of the best illustrations we possess of the general nature of a candle.

Its value as an illustration lies in the functions which it performs. Consider what the splinter does when it burns. It supplies fuel; it supplies a means of bringing that fuel to the place of chemical action; it supplies a regular and gradual flow of air to the same place; and it gives out heat and light. All these offices are united in the one material, so that candle-wood is in effect a natural candle, and we may keep it before us as the pattern against which the manufactured candles that follow are to be measured.

## Dips

The first of the manufactured kinds is the candle commonly called a _dip_. To make dips, lengths of cotton are hung up by a loop and plunged into melted tallow. Each length is then taken out and cooled, and dipped again, and cooled again, the operation being repeated over and over until a body of tallow has built up around the cotton.

## Miners' Candles

Very small candles were used by the miners in coal mines. In former times the miner had to find his own candles, and it was supposed that a small candle would not so readily set fire to the fire-damp of the mine as a large one; so that, partly for safety and partly for economy, he burned small candles, which were made at 20, 30, 40, or 60 to the pound. In time the candle gave way to the steel-mill, and the steel-mill in its turn gave way to the Davy lamp and the other safety lamps.

## A Candle from the Royal George

The next specimen bears upon durability. This candle, I am told, was taken by Colonel Pasley from the wreck of the Royal George, which had been sunk in the sea; and it lay there, exposed to the action of salt water, for many years. It shows how well candles may be preserved through long periods. Cracked and broken as it is, it burns regularly when lighted, and its tallow, once melted, returns to its natural condition.

## Materials and the Stearin Process

For many of the illustrations of candles, and of the materials of which they are made, I am indebted to Mr. Field of Lambeth.

Let us turn now to those materials. The first is suet, the fat of the ox; and it is Russian tallow, I believe, that is employed in the making of dips. A great advance was made when Gay-Lussac, or some one who shared the knowledge with him, converted the tallow into _stearin_. The difference shows itself plainly in use. The modern candle is clean, where the ordinary tallow candle is greasy; and the droppings from it may be scraped off and reduced to powder without soiling anything they touch.

The conversion of tallow into stearin is carried out in several stages.

The tallow is first boiled with quicklime, and a soap is formed; this is the process called _saponification_. The soap is then decomposed by sulphuric acid, which takes away the lime and leaves the fat rearranged as _stearic acid_. At the same time a quantity of _glycerin_ is produced, a sugar or a substance very like sugar, which comes out of the tallow in the course of this chemical change. The stearic acid is next put under pressure, and the oil is squeezed out of it; as the pressure increases, the oily part runs away and carries the impurities along with it. What remains after the pressing is melted, and cast into candles.

The candles so produced are stearin candles, made from stearin, which is itself derived from tallow.

## Other Candle Materials

There remain the other materials. Sperm candles are made from the purified oil of the spermaceti whale. Candles are made also from yellow beeswax and from refined beeswax. Paraffin, a curious substance which may be obtained from the bogs of Ireland, is likewise made into candles. Lastly there is a kind of wax brought from Japan, a new material for the candle-maker, which has reached us only since that country was forced open to outside access.

# The Candle as a Way into Natural Philosophy

In this course of lectures I propose to lay before you the chemical history of a candle. You do me the honour of coming to see our proceedings here, and I give these lectures in return; I count them a courtesy which I owe you, and I make no claim to be giving a performance.

## Why Return to the Candle

I have taken up this subject on a former occasion, and if I were left to my own will I should repeat it almost every year. The subject of the candle holds abundant interest. It is far from a narrow topic, for the candle opens onto a great many departments of philosophy. Its reach goes further still. There is no law under which any part of this universe is governed which does not come into play in the phenomena of a candle.

There is, then, no better and no more open door by which we may enter into the study of natural philosophy than the physical phenomena of a candle. The beginner needs no special apparatus to make a start. If he attends to a candle burning before him, he has enough to begin with. I shall therefore make no apology for an old topic. I am not aware of any newer topic that would serve better than the candle, and I doubt whether any would serve as well.

## Tone and Audience

Let me state the terms on which I mean to proceed. I intend to treat the subject honestly, seriously, and philosophically. I also mean to address myself to the young people rather than to the grown persons among you. I claim the privilege of speaking to the young as a young person myself, and I have spoken to young audiences in this familiar way on former occasions. I know that what I say here will be published to the world. That knowledge will not prevent me from speaking familiarly to the young listeners who are present.

## Natural Candles: Candle-Wood

Before we come to the candles which men manufacture, it may be remarked that some candles are great curiosities, and that certain kinds of trees are particularly famous for burning well. The chief example I shall offer is a substance called _candle-wood_, which is taken from some of the bogs in Ireland.

Candle-wood is a hard, strong, excellent wood, well fitted to resist force, and it burns well besides. In the places where it is found, splinters and torches are made from it. It burns like a candle and gives a very good light. For these reasons I hold it to be one of the best illustrations of the general nature of a candle.

It owes its value as an illustration to the functions it performs. Candle-wood provides fuel. It provides a means of bringing that fuel to the place of chemical action. It provides a regular and gradual supply of air to the same place. And it produces heat and light. Because one material performs all of these offices together, candle-wood is in effect a natural candle; and we may keep it in mind as a model against which to measure the manufactured candles that follow.

## Dips

The first manufactured kind is the candle commonly called a _dip_. Lengths of cotton are hung up by a loop and dipped into melted tallow. Each length is cooled and dipped again, and the process is repeated over and over until tallow has built up round the cotton.

## Miners' Candles

The miners in coal mines used very small candles. In former times every miner had to find his own candles. It was believed that a small candle would ignite the fire-damp in the mines less readily than a large one. The miners used small candles partly for safety and partly for economy, and these were made at 20, 30, 40, or 60 to the pound. In time the steel-mill took their place, and the steel-mill was afterwards displaced by the Davy lamp and other safety lamps.

## A Candle from the Royal George

My next specimen bears on the question of durability. Colonel Pasley, I am told, took this candle from the wreck of the _Royal George_. The vessel sank in the sea, and the candle lay exposed to the salt water for many years. It shows how well candles may be preserved over long periods. Though it is cracked and broken, it burns regularly when lighted, and its tallow returns to its natural condition as soon as it is melted.

## Materials and the Stearin Process

I owe many of my illustrations of candles and their materials to Mr. Field of Lambeth. We may now turn to the materials themselves.

The first is suet, which is the fat of the ox. Russian tallow, I believe, goes to the making of dips. A great advance was made when Gay-Lussac, or some one who shared the knowledge with him, converted tallow into stearin. The difference shows itself in use. The modern candle is clean, while the ordinary tallow candle is greasy, and the drippings of a modern candle may be scraped off and powdered without soiling anything.

The conversion proceeds by stages.

The tallow is first boiled with quicklime, and a soap results. The soap is then decomposed by sulphuric acid, which takes away the lime and leaves the fat rearranged as _stearic acid_. At the same time a quantity of _glycerin_ is produced. Glycerin is a sugar, or a substance very like sugar, and it comes out of the tallow in the course of this chemical change. The oil is next pressed out of the stearic acid; and as the pressure is increased, the oily part carries the impurities away with it. What remains after the pressing is melted and cast into candles.

The candles so obtained are stearin candles, made of stearin which has been derived from tallow.

## Other Candle Materials

There remain the other materials. Sperm candles come from the purified oil of the spermaceti whale. Candles are also made of yellow beeswax and of refined beeswax. Paraffin is a curious substance from which candles are made, and it may be obtained from the bogs of Ireland. Lastly, a kind of wax brought from Japan furnishes a new material for candles; it reached us only after Japan had been forced open to outside access.

candidates.text:
# The Candle as a Way into Natural Philosophy

I propose to bring before you, in the course of these lectures, the chemical history of a candle. I offer them in return for the honour you do me in coming to see our proceedings here, and I count them a courtesy which I owe you, and no performance.

## Why Return to the Candle

I have lectured on this subject on a former occasion; and were it left to my own will, I should repeat it almost every year. The subject of the candle holds abundant interest. It is by no means a narrow one, for it opens onto many different departments of philosophy. Its reach is wider still. There is not a law governing any part of this universe which does not come into play in the phenomena of a candle.

Hence I hold that there is no better, there is no more open door by which you may enter into the study of natural philosophy, than by considering the physical phenomena of a candle. The beginner needs no specialised apparatus to start with; it is enough that he attend to something burning before him. I make no apology, therefore, for bringing you an old topic. In my judgment no newer one would be better than the candle, and probably none would be as good.

## Tone and Audience

I mean to treat the subject honestly, seriously, and philosophically. I mean also to address myself to the young people, and not to the grown persons, among you. I claim the privilege of speaking to the young as a young person myself, as I have done on former occasions. I know that my words will be published to the world; but that knowledge shall not prevent me from speaking familiarly to the young listeners before me.

## Natural Candles: Candle-Wood

Before we come to manufactured candles, let me remark that some candles are great curiosities, and that certain kinds of trees are particularly famous for burning well. My chief example is a substance called _candle-wood_, taken from some of the bogs of Ireland.

Candle-wood is a hard, strong, excellent wood, well fitted to resist force, and it burns well besides. Where it is found, splinters and torches are made of it. It burns like a candle and gives a very good light. For these reasons I regard it as one of the best illustrations we can have of the general nature of a candle.

Its value as an illustration lies in the functions which it performs. It provides fuel. It provides a means of bringing that fuel to the place of chemical action, and a regular and gradual supply of air to the same place. And it produces heat and light. All these functions are combined in one material, so that candle-wood is in effect a natural candle, and we may take it as the model by which to measure the manufactured candles that follow.

## Dips

The first manufactured kind is the candle commonly called a _dip_. Lengths of cotton are hung up by a loop and dipped in melted tallow; each length is cooled and dipped again, and the dipping and cooling go on, over and over, until the tallow has built up around the cotton.

## Miners' Candles

Very small candles were used by the miners in coal mines. In former times the miner had to find his own candles. It was believed that a small candle would ignite the fire-damp of the mine less readily than a large one, and the miners used small candles partly for safety and partly for economy. These candles were made at 20, 30, 40, or 60 to the pound. In time the steel-mill took their place, and the steel-mill in its turn gave way to the Davy lamp and the other safety lamps.

## A Candle from the Royal George

My next specimen bears upon durability. Colonel Pasley is said to have taken this candle from the wreck of the _Royal George_. It had gone down with the ship, and it lay in the sea, exposed to the salt water, for many years. It shows how well candles may be preserved over long periods. Cracked and broken as it is, it burns regularly when lighted, and once melted, its tallow returns to its natural condition.

## Materials and the Stearin Process

Mr. Field, of Lambeth, has supplied me with many illustrations of candles and of the materials of which they are made. To these materials we now turn.

The first is suet, which is the fat of the ox. Russian tallow is, I believe, the kind employed in making dips. A great advance was made when Gay-Lussac, or some one who shared the knowledge with him, converted tallow into _stearin_. The difference is plain to anyone who uses the two. The modern candle is clean, whereas the ordinary tallow candle is greasy. Its drips may be scraped off and powdered without soiling anything.

The conversion proceeds by stages.

The tallow is first boiled with quicklime and made into a soap. This soap is then decomposed by sulphuric acid, which takes away the lime and leaves the fat rearranged as _stearic acid_. Glycerin is produced at the same time. It is a sugar, or a substance like sugar, and it comes out of the tallow in the course of this chemical change. The oil is next pressed out of the stearic acid, and as the pressure is increased the oily part carries the impurities away with it. What remains after pressing is melted and cast into candles.

The products of this process are stearin candles, made from stearin derived from tallow.

## Other Candle Materials

Several other materials remain. Sperm candles come from the purified oil of the spermaceti whale. Candles are made also from yellow beeswax, and from refined beeswax. Paraffin, a curious substance which may be obtained from the bogs of Ireland, is likewise made into candles. Lastly, a kind of wax brought from Japan is a new material for making candles, and it has come within our reach only since Japan was forced open to outside access.
